parsed.study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study using interviews, public-statement transcripts, arrest records, legal and historical documents, and demographic data
parsed.population_and_sample: Predominantly low-income Black residents of Lowndes County lacking functioning household septic systems; evidence includes courthouse records for at least 10 African American residents charged under the sanitation code, individual resident cases and statements, and interviews with residents and public-health professionals.
parsed.exposure: Heir-property and housing policies, unequal land conditions, septic-system regulation, and punitive enforcement of Alabama public-health sanitation law through citations, fines, arrest, threatened eviction, and incarceration.
parsed.outcome: Absent, failing, or unaffordable household sanitation systems; inability to finance or install compliant septic systems; and sanitation-related exclusion and penalties including fines, arrest, jail, bankruptcy, and threatened loss of housing.
parsed.rationale: The Public Health Enforcement section (pp. 956–961) presents empirical arrest records, resident cases, and interviews showing how sanitation-code enforcement affected access to legal, functioning septic systems and produced fines, arrest, and threatened eviction. The Land Control and Housing Availability sections (pp. 949–956) use documentary and qualitative evidence to connect property-tenure and housing institutions to residents' inability to finance or install sanitation infrastructure. The population, institutional exposures, sanitation-access outcomes, and qualitative socio-legal case-study design are sufficiently identifiable despite the absence of a standalone methods section.
